Your own public material (you are the founder it describes):

# 11-issen: sources

Back-test entry `11-issen.yaml`: Issen, an AI voice tutor for speaking a foreign language (YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2025-06-26, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44387828 (the founders' post and 271 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MIn-issen-your-personalized-ai-voice-language-tutor
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/issen

Status today: same idea ("AI realtime voice companion for language learning", YCC).

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment).**
- "We started this company after struggling to find great tools to practice speaking Japanese and French" (HN).
- The founders' own line that it is not for beginners, honoured in the segment:
  - "So basically if you are starting a new language from zero, then this is not for you?" "That's correct." (HN/44388670, HN/44388778).
  - "Quite honestly our current focus is more for B1+ students" (HN/44388888).
  - "ISSEN is more focused on intermediate and advanced students, and especially those that are willing to use a more difficult app in order to learn faster" (HN/44391572).
- Segment **[author]**, worded from these: "adults in the US learning a foreign language at intermediate level or above, not starting from zero". One CONSUMER role.
- **[author]** The founders are not US-only. US is the default market and nothing public points elsewhere.

**2. What (the job).**
- "We wanted something that would talk with us — realistically, in full conversations — and actually help us improve" (HN).
- Against streaks: apps where users are "achieving long streaks and so on, without actually getting fluent in the language" (HN).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "become able to hold a real conversation in the language".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "Having a tutor can be awesome, but there are downsides: they can be expensive (since you pay by the hour), difficult to schedule, and have a high upfront cost (finding a tutor you like often forces you to cycle through a few that you don’t)" (HN).
- "Human tutors help, but they can be costly, hard to schedule" (YCL, as summarised).
- No time or place is named. **[author]**:
  - Circumstance "they want to practise speaking the language", occasion "practice session", window {7, DAYS}, Frequency 3 to 7 days out of 7, Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80).
  - These are the smallest choice for a daily-habit product, which the founders' "instantly speak and immerse yourself" (HN) implies.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- Intermediate and advanced learners (item 1). YCL addresses people "serious about improving their foreign language skills" (as summarised).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals are the difficulties the thread itself names:
  - vocabulary: the founders' "word bank and SRS flashcards" (HN)
  - understanding natives at speed: HN/44395109's "understanding accents/pronunciations quickly enough"
  - grammar: HN/44395682's "embarrassing holes"
  - finding time: HN/44395109's 2.5 hours a weekday
- The own item, "Finding someone to speak with when it suits", is the founders' scheduling pain in a learner's words.

**5. Who pays.**
- The learner, by subscription: "Pricing: 20 min free trial, $20–29/month" (HN).
- **[author]** Buyer and payer is "Nobody else" only. The founders name no other role. One respondent (Simon Achebe) shows the spouse the thread raises: "I would have a hard time justifying an additional subscription to my wife!" (HN/44389205).

**6. Mechanism.**
- "a custom voice AI pipeline combining STT (speech-to-text), TTS (text-to-speech), LLMs, long term memory, interruptions, turn-taking" (HN).
- "a word bank and SRS flashcards for new words learned in the AI voice chats" (HN).
- "custom curriculums for each student based on goals, interests, and preferences" (HN).
- "works on web, iOS, Android" (HN).
- The `not_assumed` item "the tutor catches pronunciation mistakes" comes from the founder's own answer: "Yes we do have this issue" (HN/44389905).
- Compatibility conditions **[author]**:
  - The tested one, "They could already hold a simple conversation", is the founders' not-for-beginners line, turned into a condition.
  - "speak aloud" draws on HN/44396663, and "steady connection" on HN/44390909 ("it's all server side", HN/44390965).
- Adoption friction **[author]**:
  - The tested effort, "Talk out loud to an AI tutor", is the product's one act.
  - The intro conversation comes from "There is a structured curriculum that gets generated after the intro lesson" (HN/44389578).
- Commitment step **[author]**: "pay for one month after the trial", the first paid act after "20 min free trial" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "$20–29/month (depending on duration and specific geography)" (HN). The founder's price is $20 to $29 a month.
- Tutor cost: "$20/hour on italki on average" (YCL, as summarised; cited there from Glassdoor).
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $80 to $160 a month, is that hourly rate times one to two lessons a week (4 to 8 lessons a month). It is the smallest reading of "you pay by the hour" (HN).
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 36%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- 271 comments, many of them first-person learners. Each respondent below is traced to one.
- The thread also holds the price objection: "I found the pricing and it’s a tough sell! ChatGPT is cheaper." (HN/44389205).
- It holds the trust objection: "I think I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations or errors" (HN/44390451).

## Respondents

- Caleb Nguyen: HN/44388565 (Vietnamese; "I pay $160/mo for Vietnamese tutoring ($20 per class) … I don't have to schedule my classes"). The rescheduling is **[author]**.
- Rosa Delgado-Hart: HN/44391306 ("I currently pay $99 a month to learn Spanish from a live tutor 30 mins a day").
- Patrick Sorensen: HN/44395109 (Thai; "30 minutes every weekday doing flashcards, 45 minutes with a tutor … To save $2,700 a year") and HN/44389181.
- Yuki Brennan: HN/44396663 ("I think I'm around A2 in Japanese … I don't mind texting … but talking just makes me feel very anxious") and HN/44390432 (skipping the textbook's speaking exercises).
- Jin-ho Park: HN/44388971 ("second-gen Korean-American; my korean is weak but conversational"). The call with an aunt is **[author]**.
- Astrid Mallory: HN/44388547 and HN/44388629 (Swedish: "I can have unstructured conversations … in real life here in Sweden", wants "a guided learning experience").
- Derek Holloway: HN/44388976 (ChatGPT voice mode, "pick a random blurb in the news", "an hour long foreign language practice in Spanish while walking my husky"). His $20 a month for ChatGPT is **[author]**.
- Nikos Ferrante: HN/44388531 (Greek "as a beginner … I still got lost 5 minutes in … a long sentence in Greek about how how it is nice to hike in mountains"). He is outside the segment on purpose: beginners reached the real app.
- Laura Pennington (gate No): HN/44388467 ("lost any semblance of proficiency -- mainly because I never have a real occasion to use anything other than English").
- Mateo Lindgren: HN/44388794 ("I used italki extensively and found having a live Columbian tutor invaluable and very affordable … It would genuinely make me sad if those excellent tutors start losing work"). Medellín and $15 are **[author]**.
- Farida Haque: HN/44388539 ("Assimil courses and done lots of comprehensible input … language production is typically the weak point … plenty of lessons on iTalki"). Moving her to French is **[author]**.
- Simon Achebe: HN/44389205 ("Frantastic is absurdly expensive and it made me switch to italki … justifying an additional subscription to my wife").
- Gabriel Stein: HN/44395682 ("living in Buenos Aires for over 18 years … my pronunciations and accent is quite good … a bunch of embarrassing holes").
- Lucía Moreno: HN/44396239 (Chinese "somewhere between HSK 2 and 3 … When I babble … it cuts me off in the first eh"; a native Spanish speaker). The exchange partner is **[author]**.
- Imani Brooks: HN/44396656 ("~Japanese N4, A2 … living outside of Japan, struggle to find good opportunities to output"). Ohio is **[author]**.
- Arjun Kapoor: HN/44390909 ("I do all my language learning on the commuter trains w/o a good connection") and HN/44390855 (Urdu). Urdu as his family's language is **[author]**.
- Tobias Wren (chip): HN/44389852 ("As an intermediate German speaker"). The refusal to say more is an author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person.
- Megan Ashford: HN/44390650 (Russian; "the AI won't spot areas where you e.g. fudge a case ending or the stress on a word").
- Hassan El-Amin (gate No): author's invention, filling a gap. No commenter describes a week without wanting to practise, and a realistic gate needs one in-segment No beside the out-of-practice Laura Pennington.
- Priya Natarajan: HN/44392491 ("I don't think I can trust TTS for language learning. I could be internalizing wrong pronunciation") and HN/44390451 ("I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real person's name.

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** None of the registry's five advantage codes means "available any time". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Speaking practice any time, no tutor to book", because it drops the tutor. `shorter_time` was the other candidate.
- **YC launch wording.** The WebFetch summaries of YCL and YCC were paraphrases, not full text. The two YCL phrases above marked "as summarised" may differ slightly from the page. Every HN quote is verbatim from the thread's API text.
- **Cost estimate.** The $80 to $160 a month is my arithmetic on "$20/hour on italki on average", not a founder statement. Several respondents spend nothing, because the problem's cost to them is the missing practice, not money. So Existing sacrifice is likely to read below the founder's estimate.
- **Market.** US is assumed. Issen prices "depending on duration and specific geography", and nothing public names a US focus.
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/V. Those need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, choosing who will ask my learners the questions is an obvious step, and it sits naturally in the Before People See It stage.

screens.why3: I build voice tutors and can judge which voice my learners would talk to after hearing a 5-second sample.

screens.why3: I know whether I am messaging learners I know, working from a found list, or posting in a place like HN or a language community.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside the deciding number, 3 of 6 on relative advantage, and the card adds the bar of 4 of 6 and '1 short', so I know which belief failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives the count and the bar, but relative advantage needs a second look: 7 people answered yet it counts over 6 with no reason given, and '3 at or beyond what you said, 3 short of it' sits oddly beside '3 of 6... 3 of them a lot'.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, including 'speaking practice any time, no tutor to book'.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what a miss on 'any time, no tutor to book' means for Issen or what to do about it; the only explanatory line says how the verdict is worked out.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and nothing is claimed beyond these people, but a flat 'Did not hold' on one person short among 6 never says this is a small group, and the seventh person's absence is unexplained.
screens.instead: Did not hold, narrowly: 3 of the 6 counted said any-time practice with no tutor to book would have made their last time better, and you needed 4 (the seventh wasn't counted, and here's why). With so few people this is a warning rather than proof, so open this card to see what the other 3 said before you lean on 'no tutor to book' as the reason to switch.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so the verdict and its deciding number are tied together at the top.
screens.why_b2: The four answer rows are marked for or against, 7 people are counted, and the bar at 5 of 7 is marked on the strip, so I see all three at first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "they could already hold a simple conversation" are the name and belief I checked on the way in, awkward grammar included.
screens.why_b4: The So line clears this belief and points me to adoption friction, but it doesn't say what to change about Issen, and the clearing rests on a question that never tested conversational ability.
screens.why_b5: People were asked whether it would have fitted how things were set up, not whether they could hold a conversation, so "Holding up" and the flat "is not what will stop them" claim more than the answers can carry, and "Adoption friction, below, is" is just as flat, despite the honest n of 7 and the "a lean, not a call" note.
screens.instead: 7 of 7 said Issen would have fitted how things were set up last time they practised, but this didn't test whether they can hold a simple conversation, so that belief is still unchecked; test it directly before relying on it, including with beginners who reach the app.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly above "3 of 6 said it would have gone better, bar 4 of 6, 1 short", so I have the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 against Same 3 over 6 people and the bar at 4 are plain, but the Same row is labelled "no difference or worse" and the bar is written two ways (4 of 6, no more than 1 in 3), which takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are the Relative advantage belief I checked, word for word: speaking practice any time, no tutor to book.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and points me to the reasons below and on the Insights tab; the quotes hint at scheduling, grammar and cheap chatbots, but the screen never says what this means for the idea or what I should do.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Yuki's exclusion is explained, and the screen says outright "a small group: a lean, not a call" and that the question was a hypothetical.
screens.instead: Say what the three no-difference answers mean for me: on this small group, any-time practice doesn't beat what a tutor, immersion or a cheap chatbot already gives these people, so sharpen what Issen does that those can't before leaning on 'no tutor to book'.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 would do it, bar 5 of 7", so I know the belief held and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers across 7 people, marks each for or against, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and my bar at 5, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title and "Most would talk out loud to an AI tutor" are exactly what I checked on the way in, and the question uses the same act.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the 4 and 2 and points below, without saying what this means for Issen or naming Yuki's speaking anxiety, the one thing here I could act on.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible and "a lean, not a call" is honest, but the promise of what would make it worth it to those 2 is a soft overstatement: Astrid gave no reason and Jin-ho's is about what he'd pay, not about talking aloud.
screens.instead: Most of these 7 would talk out loud to an AI tutor, but it's a lean: only 4 would as is, and 2 would only if it was clearly worth it. Jin-ho would need to get through a whole family call, Astrid gave no reason, and Yuki is too anxious to speak yet, so prove the payoff early and ask more learners whether anxiety stops them.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict with the deciding number beside it: Did not hold at 3 of 6 against a bar of 4, 1 short, and Holding up at 6 of 7 against a bar of 5.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and both belief lines are exactly the ones I checked on the way in, including "speaking practice any time, no tutor to book".
screens.why_b4: The screen stops at the quotes and never says what the miss on relative advantage means for the idea, so I have to work out for myself whether to change the pitch, the segment or the product.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and the quotes make no claim beyond the people who said them, but a miss by one person out of 6 is a flat "Did not hold" with no word that this is a small group, and only 1 of the 2 conditional yeses is quoted under a line called Holding up.
screens.why_b6: The quotes tell me things I did not type: a cheap chatbot voice mode already does the job on dog walks, an immersed learner is stuck on grammar and words rather than speaking, a tutor's only flaw is rescheduling, anxiety blocks speaking aloud, and one learner's price depends on getting through a whole family call.
screens.instead: Relative advantage missed by 1 of 6, a small group: these three already have speaking practice that works (a chatbot, daily life, a tutor they like), so "any time, no tutor to book" gives them little; test the pitch on learners with no one to speak with, and prove it against ChatGPT voice mode.

screens.why1: As the first question it makes sense to check that I'm already speaking some of the language before asking me about practising it.
screens.why2: I can answer this straight away, since I'm learning Vietnamese and every word is one I would use myself.
screens.why3: I know exactly where my speaking stands after paying for regular Vietnamese classes.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a screener, because even a shaky speaker can honestly say they speak some, and no escape is expected on this kind of question.
screens.why5: It keeps to learners who aren't starting from zero, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with two short options, so I can hear it once and answer, even if 'I'll read 2 options' is a little stiff for a yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking if I can already speak some of the language, it makes sense to ask whether I wanted to practise it this past week, before asking for the story.
screens.why2: I'd get this on first read or first hearing, though "the language" sounds a bit stiff when I'd just say Vietnamese.
screens.why3: I have regular tutoring classes and know whether I wanted to practise speaking this week, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but "I can't recall one particular time" is odd for a question about wanting to practise, there are two escapes where one would do, and my yes leads to a story about when I practised, which doesn't fit if I only wanted to.
screens.why5: It stays with wanting to practise speaking in the last 7 days, and I see nothing about a product or company.
screens.why6: It is one short question with "Yes or no" at the end, so I can hear it once and answer straight away.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you practise speaking the language, or try to? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After being asked whether I speak some of the language and wanted to practise this week, an idea for speaking practice is the obvious next thing, and the kicker tells me it's coming.
screens.why2: I get it on first read as a learner who knows flashcards and spaced repetition, but 'custom curriculum' is app-marketing talk and 'spoken practice with flashcards' undersells what turns out to be an AI tutor.
screens.why3: I pay for Vietnamese classes and want to speak, so I can judge an AI voice tutor against what I actually do each week.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: An idea card is meant to show me the product, but the last line just repeats 'full spoken conversations' from the first sentence instead of telling me what they believe it would change for me.
screens.why6: It says without any parenthesis or slash and each sentence is short, but six sentences is a lot to hold in one hearing, 'real-time AI voice tutor' and 'spaced-repetition flashcards' are mouthfuls, and 'full spoken conversations' comes round twice.
screens.instead: Imagine Issen, an AI voice tutor for speaking practice. You hold full spoken conversations with it at your level, about your goals and interests, and the new words become flashcards. It is not for complete beginners. The people building it believe this would give you real conversation practice whenever you want it.

screens.why1: Right after being shown the idea, it makes sense to ask whether it would have worked for my last speaking practice.
screens.why2: "Fitted the way things were set up for you" is vague, and I'd have to reread it to work out whether it means my tutor, my schedule or something else.
screens.why3: I know how my last class with my tutor went, but the card only says "spoken practice with flashcards," so I'd be partly guessing whether it would have fit.
screens.why4: The scale and "I can't tell" cover my answers, but "most of the time" is odd when I'm being asked about one specific occasion.
screens.why5: No product detail leaks beyond the idea card, but "the way things were set up" is stiff, generic wording that drifts from anything about practising speaking.
screens.why6: It's short and the four options are easy to hold when heard, but "the way things were set up for you" is a hazy clause to catch in one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you practised speaking the language. Could you have used flashcards for spoken practice that time instead? Yes, easily; yes, with some hassle; only partly; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether it would have fitted my practice, it makes sense to ask whether it would have gone better with this.
screens.why2: The words are simple and I get it on first read, though "the last time" leans on the previous screen to mean my last speaking practice.
screens.why3: I know how my last tutoring class went, but all I know of Issen is "spoken practice with flashcards," so my answer about how it would have changed things is partly a guess.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover what I would say, they don't overlap, and "I can't tell" fits given how little I know about it.
screens.why5: Issen is named only as the idea on the card, and nothing about the founder's plans or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after hearing them once, and the escape comes cleanly at the end.

screens.why1: It follows straight on from my answer that Issen wouldn't have changed much, so asking what would help instead makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: I understand it on first read, but "on your last time" is clumsy and "holding a real conversation in the language" sounds a bit formal next to how I'd say speaking Vietnamese.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would help my speaking, like more tutoring hours with flexible rescheduling, so I can answer from my own classes.
screens.why4: There is only a box to type in, with no options or escape to judge.
screens.why5: Issen is fairly named after the idea card, so nothing leaks, but "holding a real conversation" reads like someone's goal statement rather than words I would use.
screens.why6: It is one clear question I can answer after one hearing, but two sentences with the awkward "on your last time" and a trailing "if anything" make it a little long to say aloud.
screens.instead: You said Issen wouldn't change much about your last practice. What would make speaking the language go better for you, if anything?

screens.why1: After being told about Issen and asked whether it would fit and help, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually be willing to do the one thing it requires, though I did just say it wouldn't make much difference.
screens.why2: Talking out loud to an AI tutor is plain to me as someone who pays for Vietnamese tutoring, and I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd speak Vietnamese out loud to an AI, since I already practise out loud with a human tutor every week.
screens.why4: The four cover my range, but 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' is a bit vague and sits close to a plain yes because anything I do has to be worth it, while 'I can't tell' fits fine as the escape.
screens.why5: It keeps to what the card says and the only thing it adds is the AI tutor, which is a fair description of how it works rather than anything odd or internal.
screens.why6: Heard once it's short, one question, with four short options I can hold and a single escape at the end.
